paras: The threatened lynching of Adam Stewart took place near Ridgely, Caroline County, Maryland, in March 1903, after Stewart, a Black farm hand, was accused of shooting his employer, John H. Imler. Facing calls to lynch him, the sheriff moved Stewart from the Denton jail to Baltimore, where he was held until his trial. Imler died on April 3, and Stewart, tried in Queen Anne's County after his lawyer sought to move the case, was sentenced to 15 years.

Stewart worked on the farm of John H. Imler, described as a well-known young farmer living several miles north of Denton. The Denton dispatch said Stewart "had manifested an ugly disposition for several days", a later Baltimore report spoke of disputes between the two men, and Stewart, according to the German-language Deutsche Correspondent, said after his arrest that Imler had not treated him right.

About 7 a.m. on Saturday, March 28, Imler went to call Stewart, and Stewart shot him in the abdomen with a pistol and fled. According to the Deutsche Correspondent, Stewart then walked downstairs and held the revolver in the face of Imler's mother when she confronted him. Imler was taken to City Hospital in Baltimore, where surgeons could not find the bullet.

A search party went after Stewart, numbered by the Denton dispatch at about fifty men, and after several hours he was found hiding in a pine thicket north of Denton and jailed there. The Deutsche Correspondent credited Sheriff Isaac L. Dukes and his men with the capture, while the Denton dispatch named Deputy Samuel Griffin.

As word spread that Imler might not survive, the Deutsche Correspondent reported, anger grew until "ernstliche Rufe laut wurden" (serious calls were heard) to lynch Stewart. Sheriff Dukes took him by carriage to Baltimore, arriving at 6 a.m. on Sunday, March 29, and Stewart was held at a station house and then in the city jail "for safe keeping". No crowd is reported to have gathered at the Denton jail.

Imler died at City Hospital early on Friday, April 3, and an inquest held that evening at Baltimore's Central Police Station heard doctors testify that he died of shock and hemorrhage from a pistol wound. Stewart admitted the shooting before the jury and was committed to await the Caroline County authorities. About 500 people attended Imler's funeral at Boonsboro, Caroline County.

Indicted for murder, Stewart was set for trial at Denton, but his counsel, William H. Dewese, said he would seek removal from Caroline County, "where great indignation was aroused by the homicide". Stewart was tried at Centreville in the Queen Anne's County circuit court and sentenced to 15 years in the penitentiary, having remained in the Baltimore jail until his trial.

Coverage came entirely from white papers in Maryland and nearby states, and no Black-press report was found. The Baltimore Deutsche Correspondent gave the fullest account, under the headline "Von einem Neger geschossen" ("Shot by a Negro"), and called Stewart "den schwarzen Schieß bold" in reporting the calls to lynch him. A Baltimore wire of March 31, run under "Shot by Colored Farm Hand" in Pennsylvania and Virginia, said Stewart had been brought to the city "to prevent a probable lynching by Imler's neighbors".

Regional weeklies in Westminster and Snow Hill printed the story among short Maryland items, and Delaware and Virginia papers carried Imler's death as a one-line digest item. None of these papers commented on the lynching threat; they mentioned it only to explain why Stewart was moved, and later why his trial was moved.

Details varied between reports: the Baltimore wire called the prisoner "John Stewart" and put the shooting on Sunday, while the Denton dispatch and later reports gave Saturday, March 28. Early reports also differed on Imler's chances, the Westminster paper reporting hope of recovery and the Deutsche Correspondent little hope.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Adam Stewart
bases: After Stewart was accused of shooting his employer, 'serious calls' to lynch him were reported in the neighborhood and the sheriff removed him to Baltimore to prevent it (A1, A2, A4, A11); no crowd or attack on the jail is reported, so this is a threatened lynching.

Three independent white reports (a Baltimore German daily, a Baltimore wire, and the Westminster weekly) agree that Stewart was moved to Baltimore because of the lynching threat (A1, A2, A4), and a later Baltimore report repeats it (A11).

accounts.label: Baltimore German daily (first report)
accounts.gist: Stewart shot Imler when Imler came to wake him, pointed the revolver at Imler's mother, and hid in the woods; after his capture he confessed, saying Imler had not treated him right, and serious calls to lynch him led the sheriff to take him to Baltimore.

accounts.label: Denton dispatch
accounts.gist: Stewart, who had shown 'an ugly disposition' for days, fired when Imler called him to the field, fled, and was caught by a deputy after a posse of about fifty searched for him.

accounts.label: Baltimore wire
accounts.gist: 'John Stewart' was in the Baltimore city jail, charged with attempting to murder his employer, having been brought there to prevent a probable lynching by Imler's neighbors.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury (inquest)
accounts.gist: Doctors testified that Imler died of a pistol wound, a signed statement from Imler named Stewart, and Stewart admitted the shooting.

framing.detail: The Baltimore German daily headed its first story 'Von einem Neger geschossen' ('Shot by a Negro') and called Stewart 'den schwarzen Schieß bold' in reporting the calls to lynch him, without comment on the threat.
Out-of-state papers ran the Baltimore wire under 'Shot by Colored Farm Hand' and a one-line death notice in news digests.
Maryland and Delaware papers carried the case as a short regional item, noting the lynching danger and the 'great indignation' in Caroline County as reasons for moving the prisoner and the trial.

conflicts.note: The Denton dispatch is dated March 28 and the later reports give March 28; the Baltimore wire's 'Sunday' is probably the day Stewart reached Baltimore.
Only the Baltimore wire uses 'John'; all other reports, including the indictment notice, say Adam.
